name: Dusty sage
lede: Dusty sage renders Aoshirotsurubami (青白橡), a traditional Japanese name meaning "pale oak", for a greyed, greenish sage.

sections.title: A pale-oak compound name
sections.body:
Our color library gives the source as 青白橡 (Aoshirotsurubami), literally built from ao (blue-green), shiro (white/pale) and tsurubami, the grey-brown dyed with acorns from the oak tree, so "pale oak" is the sense the library records [1]. No first-recorded date survives in our sources, so when the name entered use is undocumented here [1].

The nearest named color in our graph is [[sage]] itself, at a color distance (ΔE2000) of 4.2, a more vivid shade; [[gnaphalium-green]], named for the grey-leaved cudweed plant, sits the same distance away and reads duller and greener [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this sage in 503 of 23,781 paintings, about 2.1 percent, as photographed [3]. It is strongest in Impressionist painting overall, more than five times the archive average, led by Childe Hassam, whose canvases carry it at close to twenty-two times that rate, with Berthe Morisot close behind [3]. By country it is most concentrated in Nepali and Iranian work, and the earliest dated match is a Madonna and Child from 1455, a floor set by what survives and was photographed, not a first sighting [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; the figures are a color match, not a pigment identification [3].
